title: Vermont Yankee, statutory interpretation, and administrative common law
shortTitle: Vermont Yankee, statutory interpretation, and administrative common law
summary: The assigned debate asks whether disclosure, logical-outgrowth, and response duties interpret the APA’s requirements or improperly add procedures to them.
notes:
The historical introduction describes judicial efforts to require limited trial-type procedures in technically complex rulemakings. Mobil Oil reasoned that an adversarial opportunity was necessary to create evidence substantial enough for rate review even without formal rulemaking. Vermont Yankee rejected general judicial authority to add preferred procedures, but retained review of the rule’s support. The notes ask whether challenging deficient evidence differs meaningfully from demanding more opportunities to test it.

In American Radio Relay League, the D.C. Circuit required fuller disclosure of staff studies under Portland Cement. Then-Judge Kavanaugh accepted binding circuit precedent but argued separately that the requirement lacked a basis in § 553’s text and conflicted with Vermont Yankee. He also criticized the cumulative procedural and substantive demands imposed through expanding arbitrary-and-capricious review. His criticism did not erase the panel’s holding.

Ronald Levin defends evolving APA interpretation as a response to the transformation of agency rulemaking. He points to Supreme Court recognition of logical outgrowth, review on an administrative record, and responses to significant comments despite spare statutory language. His account treats the boundary between interpretation and extra-statutory procedure as contested. The reading also notes that agencies themselves may choose oral workshops and additional participation. Distinguishing Congress’s requirements, judicial interpretation, constitutional minima, and voluntary agency choices prevents the debate from collapsing into an absolute ban on every procedure beyond § 553’s literal words.
